subject: chemistry
question_text: Discuss the pattern of variation in the oxidation states of boron to thallium.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Boron and aluminium
lines: Group 13 elements have the valence shell
configuration ns²np¹, so the group
oxidation state is +3.
For boron the sum of the first three
ionisation enthalpies is very high, so it
does not form B³⁺; it bonds covalently.
That sum falls considerably from boron to
aluminium, so aluminium forms Al³⁺.
steps.why: The +3 state comes from using all three valence electrons of ns²np¹. Whether an element reaches that state as an ion depends on the energy needed to remove the three electrons, which is why boron stays covalent and aluminium does not.
common_mistakes: Writing that boron forms B³⁺ ions. Removing three electrons from so small an atom costs too much energy, so boron bonds covalently.
Giving no oxidation state for boron at all. Boron does show +3, by sharing rather than by losing electrons.
steps.memory_tip: Three valence electrons ns²np¹ give +3. Boron is too small to lose all three, so it shares them.
steps.margin_note: Write the configuration ns²np¹ before naming the states.

steps.label: Gallium, indium and thallium
lines: Gallium, indium and thallium show both
+3 and +1 oxidation states.
Going down the group the +1 state becomes
steadily more stable, in the order
Al < Ga < In < Tl.
That order compares the +1 state of one
element with the +1 state of the next.
For thallium the +1 state is the more
stable of the two; for aluminium, gallium
and indium the +3 state is still the
stable one.
The reason is the inert pair effect: the
ns² electron pair takes less and less
part in bonding down the group.
steps.why: The +1 state appears because the ns² pair can be left out of bonding while only the single np¹ electron is used. That pair is held more tightly down the group, so +1 grows steadily more stable from aluminium to thallium.
common_mistakes: Writing that only thallium shows +1. Gallium and indium show it as well, though for them +3 is still the stable state.
Reversing the order and writing that +3 becomes more stable down the group.
steps.memory_tip: The heavier the element, the more the ns² pair stays out of bonding: +1 stability runs Al < Ga < In < Tl.
steps.margin_note: The order Al < Ga < In < Tl and the words inert pair effect both belong in this step.

insider_note: The question asks for a pattern, so the answer needs both ends of the group: why boron and aluminium give only +3, and why +1 appears and grows more stable from gallium to thallium.
